Patients with <or =5 metastatic sites in prostate cancer tend to have better survival rates than those with >5 lesions. This suggests that early detection and aggressive treatment of patients with a small number of metastatic lesions may be beneficial for improving long-term survival.

In other words, having only a few (usually fewer than 5) metastatic sites can indicate an earlier stage of cancer or even a localized disease, which may respond well to more intensive treatments. This does not mean that all patients with oligometastases are treated aggressively or have better outcomes, but rather that their cancers might be more amenable to early intervention and possibly more responsive to treatment strategies focused on reducing the number of metastatic sites.

It is essential to note that this conclusion is based on studies that looked at very specific subsets of patients (those with <or =5 metastatic sites vs. those with >5 lesions) and should not be applied universally to all prostate cancer patients. Additionally, various factors, such as overall health status, quality-of-life concerns, and preferences regarding treatment options, can influence a patient's decision-making process for their care.
